extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of philosophy (readers of Kant); theologians and historians of ideas
extracted.subtask_description: Extracting and explicating Kant's criteria and principles for judging purposiveness, teleology, and the limits of physico-theology in nature (from the Critique of Judgment). Focuses on when we may legitimately call natural things means or final purposes and what follows for inferences about a World Cause.

rubrics_metrics.name: External purposiveness
rubrics_metrics.description: By external purposiveness I mean that by which one thing of nature serves another as means to a purpose. Things which have no internal purposiveness (e.g. earth, air, water) may at the same time be very purposive externally, i.e. in relation to other beings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Only when the recipient is an organised being (a natural purpose) can we judge other things as means to it. If the recipient is not organised, we cannot represent its cause under the predicate of a means. Examples and anti-patterns: do not treat mountains as 'means' if they contain nothing that requires a ground of possibility according to purposes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Internal purposiveness (natural purpose)
rubrics_metrics.description: Internal purposiveness is bound up with the possibility of an object being itself a purpose; we can ask about an organised being: 'What is it for?' and represent its internal possibility by a causality according to purposes, a creative Understanding, i.e. design.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Internal purposiveness presupposes that the object's possibility is represented through final causes and an Idea lying at its ground. This is distinct from merely attributing external utility: internal purposiveness makes the organism a 'natural purpose' and grounds teleological explanation for its form and organization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between internal and external purposiveness
rubrics_metrics.description: External purposiveness (one thing serving another as means) is quite different from internal purposiveness (an object's being a purpose in itself), and only organised beings can be final purposes; external purposiveness presupposes an organised recipient.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When judging nature teleologically, consistently maintain this distinction: do not conflate mechanical functioning of non-organised natural objects with purposiveness proper; ensure that 'means' judgments refer to organised ends.

rubrics_metrics.name: Criteria for calling something a final purpose
rubrics_metrics.description: A final purpose is that purpose which needs no other as condition of its possibility; it is unconditioned. A thing to be a final purpose must be of a kind dependent on no further condition than merely its Idea.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Final purpose cannot be found among empirical natural objects because everything in nature is conditioned; only a noumenal (moral) being can be so conceived. Do not label empirically conditioned ends as final purposes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Man as (candidate for) ultimate purpose of nature (conditions)
rubrics_metrics.description: Man is the only being on earth who can form a concept of purposes and by Reason make an aggregate of purposively formed things a system of purposes; considered as noumenon and moral being, man can be the final purpose of nature insofar as he can be an end in himself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This status requires placing the ultimate purpose in man's noumenal capacities (freedom, moral legislation). We cannot ground such a final purpose purely in empirical facts about 'man' as a natural organism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Culture (rather than earthly happiness) as nature's ultimate end regarding humanity
rubrics_metrics.description: If nature has an ultimate purpose in respect to the human race, it is the production of the aptitude for arbitrary purposes in general (culture), not the attainment of man's empirical happiness. Culture produces the formal subjective condition of setting purposes at all.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish between 'culture of skill' (development of faculties and arts) and 'culture of discipline' (freeing the will from despotism of desires). Only discipline (training of the will) relates to the formation of the will and so to true final ends.

rubrics_metrics.name: Culture of skill vs culture of discipline
rubrics_metrics.description: The culture of skill is the development of capacities to further one's purposes (aptitude in using nature), whereas the culture of training (discipline) is negative and consists in freeing the will from the despotism of desires; both play different roles in the teleological account.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that skill requires inequality and social arrangements; discipline is what makes the will receptive to higher, non-natural ends. For attributing an ultimate purpose to nature, emphasize discipline (formation of freedom) rather than mere technical skill or luxury.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use and limits of teleological (reflective) judgment
rubrics_metrics.description: Teleological principles are principles of the reflective Judgement: they do not determine the origin of organic beings but are conditions of how our Understanding must represent them. They provide a regulative outlook over nature but do not furnish constitutive explanations of origins.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: It is legitimate and often invited to attempt mechanical explanations, but teleological judgment is a subjective condition of our cognitive faculty when we seek unity of nature's forms. Do not mistake teleological judgment for an empirical causal theory of origins.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limits of mechanistic explanations and the concept of a formative impulse
rubrics_metrics.description: Kant acknowledges the permissibility and invitation to try mechanical (physico-mechanical) explanations of organic forms, but regards the spontaneous self-organization of crude matter into purposive, self-maintaining forms as contradictory to Reason; he allows an undeterminable element (a 'formative impulse') in organised matter distinct from merely mechanical formative power.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When attempting reductionist accounts, remember Kant's caution: even the most audacious mechanical attempts are permitted but one should recognize that our Understanding may not attain the origin of purposive forms by mechanism alone; avoid asserting that mechanism exhausts teleological explanation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Physico-theology: scope and empirical limits
rubrics_metrics.description: Physico-theology is the endeavour to infer a Supreme Cause of nature and its properties from the purposes of nature (empirically known). It can justify a concept of an intelligent World Cause as a subjective concept for our judgement, but it cannot determine a final purpose of creation nor deduce the full properties of a Deity beyond what experience reveals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not treat physico-theology as sufficient to ground a full Theology: empirical teleology can suggest intelligence but cannot provide a determinate concept of a supreme Being, because empirical data cannot survey the whole of nature as a system nor establish unconditioned ends.

rubrics_metrics.name: Theoretical reason cannot establish a determinate concept of Deity; practical reason supplements it
rubrics_metrics.description: From the theoretical (empirical) use of Reason alone we cannot derive the concept of a Deity adequate for teleological judging of nature. An Idea of a Supreme Being that supplements the defective empirical representation rests fundamentally a priori in our practical use of Reason (moral theology).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When attempting to infer divine attributes or final designs, be explicit about the inferential source: claims going beyond empirical evidence require the practical (moral) use of Reason and cannot be validated solely by physico-theological argument.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unity/system of natural purposes cannot be grounded within nature
rubrics_metrics.description: If we seek an objective ultimate purpose in nature as a teleological system, experience flatly contradicts the maxims of Reason: no natural being in the world can make claim to the eminence of being the final purpose of creation; an ultimate purpose cannot be discovered within nature itself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid positing a natural ultimate purpose found purely by surveying empirical nature; teleological unification of natural purposes requires a supersensible principle outside nature (or the noumenal standpoint) and cannot be settled by empirical inspection alone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Caution about extending limited empirical teleology into full theological claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Because the principles for determining the concept of an intelligent World Cause are merely empirical, we cannot justifiably add arbitrary supplements to make it an Allwise, Infinite Being; to do so would exceed the theoretical use of Reason which ought not to ascribe more properties than empirical data warrant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be wary of extrapolating an 'Allwise' Deity from partial teleological evidence. If one supplements the empirical concept, justify such supplements by appeal to moral/practical grounds rather than pretending they are produced by theoretical cognition of nature.
